title: Hell and the Final Fate of the Lost
question: What is the final fate of the lost?
intro:
Every Christian tradition confesses that Christ will judge the living and the dead, and that rejecting God carries a real and terrible outcome. The disagreement is over what that outcome finally is. Three answers have serious biblical and historical defenders: the lost suffer consciously and without end (eternal conscious torment); the lost are punished and then cease to exist, because immortality is a gift given only in Christ (conditional immortality or annihilationism); or hell is a severe but remedial fire through which God will finally bring every person to repentance and reconciliation (Christian universalism or restorationism).

The debate turns on a handful of questions: what the Greek adjective *aiōnios* (usually 'eternal' or 'everlasting') means when it qualifies punishment, fire and destruction; whether the human soul is naturally immortal; how the New Testament's 'all' texts (Rom 5:18, 1 Cor 15:22-28, Col 1:20) relate to its warnings of exclusion; and what divine justice and love require. Church history is also contested, especially whether the Second Council of Constantinople (553) condemned universal restoration as such or only a specific Origenist cosmology.

positions.name: Eternal conscious torment
positions.summary: The lost are raised at the last judgment and sent, body and soul, into a punishment that is conscious and never ends. Hell is the just response of a holy God to sin against his infinite worth; there is no repentance or release after judgment, and the endlessness of the punishment mirrors the endlessness of the life given to the redeemed.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa; theologian
figures.bio: Augustine's *City of God* gave the Latin West its most thorough defense of endless punishment. In Book 21 he argues that bodies can burn without being consumed, answers those he calls 'the merciful' who hoped hell would end for some or all, and insists that 'eternal' must mean the same thing for punishment as it does for life in Matt 25:46. His framework shaped medieval and Reformation teaching alike.

works.author: Augustine
works.title: Enchiridion (Handbook on Faith, Hope and Love)

figures.name: Thomas Aquinas
figures.profession: Dominican friar and university theologian (Paris, Naples)
figures.bio: Aquinas gave the classic scholastic argument that the gravity of an offense is measured partly by the dignity of the one offended, so that mortal sin against God merits a punishment unending in duration. He also argued that the damned, being fixed in their will after death, never cease to turn from God. The relevant questions on hell in the Supplement to the *Summa* were compiled from his earlier writings by his students after his death.

positions.context:
From the second century onward many Christian writers spoke of 'eternal fire' for the wicked (for example the *Martyrdom of Polycarp* and Justin Martyr), though early writers did not always state precisely whether it involved endless consciousness. By the fifth century, largely through Augustine, endless conscious punishment had become the majority view in the West, and it was the dominant view in the East as well.

It was given confessional form repeatedly: the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) spoke of perpetual punishment with the devil; the Augsburg Confession (1530, art. 17) rejected the idea that the punishments of the condemned would end; the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 33) speaks of everlasting torments. The *Catechism of the Catholic Church* (1992, §1033–1037) teaches the eternity of hell while describing its chief pain as eternal separation from God. Eastern Orthodox writers generally affirm hell's endlessness, sometimes describing it as the experience of God's unchanging love by those who refuse it. Modern evangelical defenses (Peterson, Morgan, Burk) were written largely in response to the conditionalist revival after John Stott's 1988 statement.
claims: Every human being will exist forever, either in fellowship with God or under his judgment.
Matt 25:46 places 'eternal punishment' and 'eternal life' in parallel; if one is unending, so is the other.
The punishment of the lost is conscious: Scripture speaks of weeping, gnashing of teeth, and no rest day or night.
There is no opportunity for repentance after death or after the final judgment.
Hell is fundamentally just: sin is an offense against an infinitely holy God and deserves an unending penalty.
Hell is shared with the devil and his angels, whose torment is explicitly said to be 'for ever and ever'.
The reality of hell magnifies the grace of the cross and gives urgency to mission.

scriptures.reading: The same adjective (aiōnios) qualifies both punishment and life in one sentence; the punishment lasts as long as the life does.
The lost share the 'eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels', whose torment Rev 20:10 calls unending.
The smoke of their torment rises for ever and ever and they have no rest day or night: language of ongoing experience, not a single moment of extinction.
The devil, beast and false prophet are tormented day and night for ever; the lost are cast into the same lake of fire.
The worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; Jesus warns of an enduring state in Gehenna.
Some rise to everlasting life, some to everlasting shame and contempt; shame and contempt imply continuing subjects.
The rich man is conscious, in anguish, and separated by a fixed chasm; even if a parable, it assumes conscious post-mortem punishment.
'Everlasting destruction away from the presence of the Lord' describes ruin and exclusion, a state the person undergoes, not non-existence.
Weeping and gnashing of teeth presupposes conscious suffering.

arguments.text: The parallel in Matt 25:46 is decisive: interpreters cannot shorten the punishment without, on the same grammar, shortening the life.
Revelation explicitly describes conscious, unending torment for the devil and his allies, and assigns the lost to the same lake of fire.
Jesus, not Paul or John, speaks most often and most vividly about Gehenna, outer darkness and unquenchable fire.
The seriousness of an offense depends partly on the dignity of the one wronged; sin against the infinitely holy God therefore merits an unending penalty.
The lost do not stop sinning after death; continued rebellion incurs continued just punishment.
Endless punishment has been the majority teaching of the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches for most of Christian history and appears in their confessions.
Second Temple Jewish texts (for example parts of *1 Enoch* and 4 Maccabees) already spoke of enduring punishment, so Jesus' hearers would naturally have understood his language that way.

critiques.text: The view depends on an assumption of natural immortality of the soul that comes more from Greek philosophy than from Scripture, which says God alone has immortality and that it is given as a gift.

Scripture's dominant vocabulary for the fate of the lost is destruction, perishing, death and burning up; 'eternal punishment' can mean a punishment whose result (death) is eternal, just as 'eternal redemption' in Heb 9:12 is a once-for-all act with eternal results.

Unending torment for sins committed in a finite life is disproportionate, and it means evil is never defeated but preserved forever in God's creation, contradicting the promise that God will be all in all.

responses.text: The traditional view does not need Platonic immortality. God sustains the lost in existence by his will; the argument rests on Jesus' and John's descriptions of enduring punishment, not on a theory of the soul. Many defenders explicitly grant that only God has inherent immortality.

Destruction and death in Scripture often mean ruin or loss of proper function rather than non-existence (e.g. the 'lost' sheep or son, the 'ruined' wineskins). And Rev 14 and 20 describe ongoing experience, which result-only readings struggle to explain.

Proportion is measured by the dignity of the one offended and the ongoing character of rebellion, not by the time it took to commit a sin. Evil is defeated in hell: it is contained, judged and no longer able to harm, which is how God is all in all.

strawMen.strawMan: Traditionalists believe God enjoys torturing people.
strawMen.correction: Defenders hold that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and that hell is the just upholding of moral order, not sadism. Many stress that the lost choose separation from God.

strawMen.strawMan: Traditionalists think hell is a literal underground furnace run by demons.
strawMen.correction: Most serious defenders treat fire and worm as real but figurative descriptions of a terrible reality; Satan is a prisoner in hell, not its ruler.

strawMen.strawMan: The view rests on medieval art and Dante rather than on the Bible.
strawMen.correction: Its case is exegetical, built on Matt 25, Mark 9 and Revelation, and predates medieval imagery by many centuries.

positive: Takes Jesus' warnings with full seriousness and fuels urgency in evangelism and missions.
Underlines the gravity of sin and the magnitude of what the cross accomplished.
Affirms that moral choices have permanent weight and that justice will be fully done.
negative: Has at times been preached manipulatively, producing fear-driven faith and religious trauma.
Raises acute questions of theodicy that some believers find faith-threatening.
Vivid imagery has sometimes overshadowed the gospel's emphasis on grace.

sequence: At death the soul survives and enters a conscious intermediate state: rest with Christ for believers, distress and awaiting judgment for the lost.
At Christ's return all the dead are raised bodily.
All stand before Christ's judgment; those not united to Christ are condemned, with degrees of punishment according to their works.
The lost are cast, body and soul, into Gehenna, the lake of fire, together with the devil and his angels.
Their punishment is conscious and never ends; there is no repentance, release or annihilation.
The redeemed enjoy eternal life in the new creation, where God's justice and mercy are both displayed forever.

positions.name: Conditional immortality (annihilationism)
positions.summary: Immortality belongs to God alone and is given to human beings only as a gift in Christ. The unsaved will be raised, judged and punished in proportion to their guilt, and then finally destroyed: the 'second death' is a real and permanent end of existence. The punishment is eternal in its result, not an endless process of suffering.

figures.name: Arnobius of Sicca
figures.profession: North African rhetorician and Christian convert
figures.bio: Arnobius, writing against pagan critics around 300, argued that souls are not immortal by nature and that those who do not know God are eventually consumed and brought to nothing. He is often cited as an early witness to something like conditionalism, though his theology was idiosyncratic and he wrote as a recent convert, so how representative he was is debated.

figures.name: Edward White
figures.profession: English Congregational minister
figures.bio: White's *Life in Christ* was the most influential nineteenth-century English statement of conditional immortality, arguing that eternal life is the gift of the incarnate Christ and that the unredeemed finally perish. He remained within mainstream Congregationalism and later chaired the Congregational Union.

figures.name: John R. W. Stott
figures.profession: Anglican rector of All Souls, Langham Place, London; evangelical leader
figures.bio: In a published dialogue with the liberal Anglican David Edwards, Stott said, tentatively and with reluctance, that he found the case for the final annihilation of the impenitent to be scripturally stronger than he had assumed, while urging that it be held without dogmatism. Because of his standing, the remark opened the question for many evangelicals.

works.title: Evangelical Essentials: A Liberal-Evangelical Dialogue

figures.name: Edward William Fudge
figures.profession: American lawyer and lay theologian (Churches of Christ background)
figures.bio: Fudge's *The Fire That Consumes* surveyed the Old Testament, intertestamental literature, the New Testament and the Fathers to argue that the lost are finally destroyed. Revised through three editions, it became the standard scholarly-popular case for conditionalism and was later dramatized in the film *Hell and Mr. Fudge* (2012).

works.title: Two Views of Hell

positions.context:
Some scholars read hints of conditionalism in early writers such as Ignatius, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, who stressed that the soul lives because God wills it; others think this reads too much into them. Arnobius (c. 300) is the clearest early example. The view resurfaced among some Socinians and radical reformers, and in the nineteenth century among English Congregationalists (Edward White) and Anglicans, and in Adventist and Christadelphian movements, where it is tied to 'soul sleep' between death and resurrection.

Its evangelical revival came in the 1980s and 1990s through Fudge, John Wenham, Philip Hughes, Clark Pinnock and John Stott. A 2000 report from the UK Evangelical Alliance (ACUTE) judged it a significant minority evangelical view and not a mark of heterodoxy. Today it is promoted by the Rethinking Hell network and held by a growing number of evangelical scholars.
claims: Only God has inherent immortality; human beings receive unending life as a gift through union with Christ.
The lost are raised and judged, and suffer punishment proportionate to their sins.
The final punishment is destruction: the second death is a real, permanent end of conscious existence.
'Eternal punishment' and 'eternal destruction' describe an outcome that is irreversible, not an endless process.
Fire, worm and smoke imagery is drawn from Old Testament scenes of total destruction (Isa 66, Sodom).
Evil and its agents will be eliminated, leaving a cosmos without rebellion.

scriptures.reading: God can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna: the soul is not indestructible.
The contrast is between perishing and eternal life, not between two modes of everlasting existence.
The wages of sin is death; the gift of God is eternal life. Life itself is the gift.
Eternal punishment is the punishment of eternal death; like 'eternal redemption' (Heb 9:12) and 'eternal judgment' (Heb 6:2), aiōnios here describes a result that is never reversed.
The penalty is 'everlasting destruction', an irreversible ruin.
Quoting Isa 66:24, Jesus pictures undying worms and unquenchable fire consuming corpses: the fire cannot be put out until it has finished its work.
Sodom and Gomorrah underwent 'the punishment of eternal fire', a fire that destroyed them completely and is not still burning.
The lake of fire is explicitly named 'the second death'.
The wicked become stubble and ashes under the feet of the righteous.
God alone has immortality.

arguments.text: The Bible's dominant vocabulary for the fate of the lost is death, destruction, perishing, being consumed and burned up; it is most natural to take these terms at face value.
Immortality is presented as something to be sought and given, not something every human already has.
Eternal fire in Jude 1:7 and the unquenchable fire of Isa 66:24 refer to fires that destroy completely, showing that 'eternal fire' language does not require endless burning of living victims.
Punishment proportionate to sin fits a finite period of suffering followed by death, avoiding the problem of infinite punishment for finite wrongs.
A universe in which rebellious creatures exist forever would leave a permanent pocket of evil, which sits uneasily with God being all in all.
Belief in the inherent immortality of the soul entered Christian theology through Platonism; some early Fathers stressed that souls live only by God's will.

critiques.text: Rev 14:11 and Rev 20:10 describe torment day and night for ever and ever; a punishment that leaves no conscious subject cannot be described as having 'no rest'.
Destruction language in Scripture often means ruin rather than non-existence, and Matt 25:46 calls the result 'punishment' (kolasis), which naturally implies someone experiencing it.
Annihilation means God permanently loses creatures he loves and wills to save; it is a defeat of divine love even if not of divine power, and it leaves the 'all' texts unfulfilled.

responses.text: Rev 14:11 echoes Isa 34:9-10, where Edom's smoke rises forever as a sign of permanent desolation, not ongoing suffering. Rev 20:10 concerns the devil, beast and false prophet (the latter two symbolic powers); for human beings the lake of fire is defined as 'the second death' (Rev 20:14).

Capital punishment is still punishment even though it ends the life of the one punished. Kolasis can denote a penalty whose outcome is permanent; Jesus himself explains the alternative to life as perishing.

God's will that all be saved does not override the reality of human refusal; Scripture repeatedly warns of final loss. The 'all' texts describe a cosmos fully reconciled, which annihilation achieves by removing rebellion, not by saving every individual.

strawMen.strawMan: Annihilationists deny that the wicked are punished at all; they simply blink out at death.
strawMen.correction: Evangelical conditionalists affirm resurrection, judgment and proportionate punishment before final destruction. The 'eternal punishment' is the irreversible death that follows.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a soft, sentimental view invented to make Christianity more palatable.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders argue from the Bible's vocabulary and its doctrine of immortality, often against their own emotional preferences; Stott's statement was notably reluctant.

strawMen.strawMan: Conditionalism is a cult doctrine because Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses hold it.
strawMen.correction: It has been held by mainstream evangelical leaders and was judged by the UK Evangelical Alliance (2000) to be within the bounds of evangelical belief. Sharing one view with a group does not entail its other views.

positive: Reduces a major theodicy objection while keeping final judgment real and serious.
Encourages close attention to the biblical vocabulary of life and death.
Presents a final cosmos in which evil is wholly eliminated.
negative: Critics argue it weakens the urgency of evangelism by making the final loss seem less dreadful.
It has sometimes been a step toward broader revision of traditional doctrine for those who adopt it.
It stands against the majority confessional tradition, creating tension in confessional churches.

At Christ's return all the dead are raised, the righteous and the unrighteous.
All are judged; those in Christ receive the gift of immortality and eternal life.

positions.name: Christian universalism (restorationism)
positions.summary: God will finally bring every human being to repentance, faith and reconciliation through Christ. Hell is real and may be long and severe, but its fire is purifying and corrective rather than endless; the 'restoration of all things' (apokatastasis) means that in the end no one is lost. Salvation is only through Christ, but his saving work does not fail for anyone.

figures.name: Origen of Alexandria
figures.profession: Alexandrian biblical scholar, teacher and theologian
figures.bio: Origen taught that God's punishments are medicinal and that the end will be like the beginning, when all rational beings are restored to unity with God through Christ. His speculative framework, including the pre-existence of souls, was later controversial, and how definitely he held universal restoration (especially for the devil) is itself debated.

figures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
figures.profession: Bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia; one of the Cappadocian Fathers
figures.bio: Gregory, a pillar of Nicene orthodoxy, described the fire of judgment as a refining process that separates evil from the soul, after which all will join in thanksgiving to God. He was never condemned, and he is the strongest patristic witness that restoration could be held by an honored orthodox bishop.

works.title: On the Soul and the Resurrection

figures.name: George MacDonald
figures.profession: Scottish novelist, poet and Congregational minister
figures.bio: MacDonald lost his pastorate partly over his theology. In his sermons and fantasies he presented God as a Father whose consuming fire burns away sin precisely because he will not give up on his children. C. S. Lewis, who did not share his universalism, called MacDonald his master.

figures.name: David Bentley Hart
figures.profession: Eastern Orthodox theologian, philosopher and translator
figures.bio: Hart argues that if God creates freely, knowing every outcome, then an eternal hell would be part of what God chose in creating, which he holds is incompatible with God being goodness itself. He also argues that a will that truly sees the Good cannot reject it forever, so freedom properly understood ends in God.

positions.context:
Clement of Alexandria and Origen spoke of corrective divine punishment, and Gregory of Nyssa, Didymus the Blind, Evagrius and some Syriac writers (Isaac of Nineveh is often cited) taught or hoped for universal restoration. Augustine reports that many in his day held some form of it. In 543 Emperor Justinian issued an edict against Origen, and fifteen anathemas against Origenist teachings are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553). Whether those anathemas were formally adopted by the council, and whether they condemned universal salvation as such or a specific Origenist system (pre-existent souls, a return to a primal unity of minds), is debated among historians.

The view revived among some Pietists and Anabaptists, in eighteenth-century English and American Universalism, and among nineteenth-century figures such as F. D. Maurice and George MacDonald. In the twentieth century Karl Barth's theology of election and Hans Urs von Balthasar's 'hope' that all may be saved reopened the question. Recent philosophical and evangelical defenders include Thomas Talbott, Robin Parry, Ilaria Ramelli (whose historical work argues for wide patristic support) and David Bentley Hart. It should be distinguished from pluralist universalism, which does not hold that salvation is through Christ.
claims: God truly wills the salvation of every person, and his will is ultimately effective.
Christ's death and resurrection are the sole ground of salvation for all.
Hell is real and serious, but its fire is purifying and corrective rather than merely retributive and endless.
Repentance and faith remain possible after death; no one is saved without them.
The 'all' of Adam's fall is matched by the 'all' of Christ's restoration.
Aiōnios means 'of the age to come', not necessarily 'without end', when applied to punishment.
God's final victory is the reconciliation of all things, so that God is all in all.

scriptures.reading: As one trespass led to condemnation for all, one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all: the second 'all' is as wide as the first.
All who die in Adam will be made alive in Christ, every enemy is subjected, and God becomes all in all.
God reconciles all things to himself through the blood of the cross, things on earth and in heaven.
Every knee bows and every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord to the glory of God, a confession Paul elsewhere links with salvation (Rom 10:9).
Peter speaks of the 'restoration of all things' (apokatastasis pantōn) promised by the prophets.
God is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe: all, not only believers, are in view.
God desires all to be saved, and Christ gave himself a ransom for all.
God has consigned all to disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.
The Lord will not cast off forever; though he causes grief, he will have compassion.
The kings of the earth, earlier God's enemies, bring their glory into the city whose gates are never shut.

arguments.text: Paul's Adam-Christ parallels set the scope of salvation as wide as the scope of sin; restricting the second 'all' while keeping the first universal breaks the parallel.
The New Testament repeatedly describes the end as the reconciliation or summing up of all things in Christ, not as a permanently divided cosmos.

Aiōnios derives from aiōn ('age') and can mean 'pertaining to the age to come'; kolasis was used of corrective punishment. Matt 25:46 can therefore describe age-long correction rather than endless torment.

If God is perfectly loving and all-powerful and knows every outcome, creating persons whom he knows will be lost forever would make their loss part of his purpose; a perfectly good God would not create on those terms.
True freedom is the ability to reach one's end in the Good; a will fully informed and healed cannot reject God forever, so unending refusal is not a sustainable free choice.

Gregory of Nyssa, an honored Nicene Father, taught restoration and was never condemned; the anathemas of 553 arguably target a particular Origenist system rather than the hope of universal salvation itself.

critiques.text: Matt 25:46 uses the same aiōnios for punishment and life; if the punishment ends, consistency suggests the life could end too. The New Testament never describes anyone escaping Gehenna or the lake of fire.

Universalism reads the 'all' texts in isolation from their context: in Rom 5:17 and 1 Cor 15:23 the reconciled are 'those who receive' grace and 'those who belong to Christ'. Scripture's consistent alternative is life or destruction, not life now or life later.
Universalism undermines the urgency of Jesus' warnings and of mission, and the Church formally rejected apokatastasis at Constantinople in 553.

responses.text: Aiōnios takes its meaning from what it qualifies: the life of the age to come is endless because God's life is endless, while correction of the age to come lasts as long as it achieves its purpose. Revelation's final scenes picture open gates and the nations healed.
Universalists agree that only those who belong to Christ are saved; they hold that in the end all will come to belong to him, which is why 1 Cor 15:28 can end with God all in all.

Hell remains a real and fearful prospect in this view, so the warnings retain their force; mission flows from love, not only fear. Historians debate whether the 553 anathemas were conciliar acts and whether they targeted restoration as such or Origenist cosmology.

strawMen.strawMan: Universalists believe all religions are equally valid and Jesus is optional.
strawMen.correction: Christian universalists hold that salvation is only through Christ and requires repentance and faith; they differ on when and how all come to that faith, not on whether Christ is necessary.

strawMen.strawMan: Universalists deny hell and judgment.
strawMen.correction: Most affirm a real, possibly very long and painful hell; they deny only that it is endless and purposeless.

strawMen.strawMan: Universalism is a modern liberal invention.
strawMen.correction: Forms of it were taught by Origen and Gregory of Nyssa in the third and fourth centuries, whatever one concludes about later condemnations.

negative: Critics argue it blunts evangelistic urgency and the moral weight of present choices.

God becomes all in all, with no creature finally lost.

readings.reading: The parallel 'eternal punishment' and 'eternal life' requires equal duration: both are unending, and punishment implies a conscious subject.
Both are eternal, but the punishment is eternal death, a permanent result, just as eternal redemption (Heb 9:12) is a once-for-all act with permanent effect.
Aiōnios means 'of the age to come'; kolasis is corrective. The verse contrasts life and correction in the coming age without fixing the correction's length.
Unending smoke and 'no rest day or night' describe continuous conscious torment of worshippers of the beast.
The image echoes Isa 34:9-10 (Edom's eternal smoke after its destruction); the rising smoke is a memorial of completed judgment, and 'no rest' describes the period of suffering, not its endlessness.
The scene occurs 'in the presence of the Lamb', the one who reconciles; it describes the age-long burning of judgment, which Revelation later follows with healed nations.
The devil and his allies are tormented forever, and the lost are cast into the same place; their fate is the same.
For humans the lake of fire is defined as 'the second death'; Death and Hades are thrown in and cease to exist, showing what the lake does.
The lake of fire is real but not the last word; Rev 21–22 follows with the nations entering the city and leaves room for the healing of all.
The undying worm and unquenched fire describe an enduring state that the lost undergo.
Isa 66:24, which Jesus quotes, pictures corpses being consumed; the fire is unquenchable in that no one can stop it until it has destroyed.
Fire in Mark 9:49 also 'salts' everyone; the image is of a searing, purifying judgment, not an endless torture chamber.
'Everlasting destruction away from the presence of the Lord' is unending ruin and exclusion, experienced consciously.
'Everlasting destruction' (olethros aiōnios) is the permanent end of the person; destruction is the plain meaning.
Olethros is used in 1 Cor 5:5 of a destruction of the flesh that leads to salvation; the 'destruction of the age' can be remedial.
'All' means all who are in Christ, as v. 17 limits it to 'those who receive' grace; Paul is contrasting two heads, not promising universal salvation.
Christ's act is sufficient for all and offered to all, but only those who receive it live; others perish.
The two 'alls' are parallel in grammar and scope: everyone condemned in Adam will be justified and given life in Christ.
'Made alive' refers to resurrection of believers ('those who belong to Christ'); subjecting enemies means conquering them, not converting them.
The last enemy, death, is destroyed; God is all in all because every rebel has been removed.
All in Adam die and all in Christ are made alive; God becoming all in all describes a universe in which no one remains estranged.
Every knee bows, but some bow in defeat; confession is forced acknowledgment, as conquered enemies acknowledge a victor.
Every creature confesses Christ at the judgment before the lost are destroyed; the confession vindicates Christ, not the confessors.
The confession is 'to the glory of God the Father' and uses the language of Isa 45:23-24, where those who bow are saved; it is a genuine, saving confession.

timeline.title: Early 'eternal fire' language
timeline.note: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* and Justin Martyr speak of eternal fire and punishment for the wicked, though how they understood its duration and nature is discussed.

timeline.title: Origen's On First Principles
timeline.note: Origen presents punishment as medicinal and the end as a restoration of rational beings to God.

timeline.title: Arnobius on mortal souls
timeline.note: Arnobius argues that souls are not inherently immortal and that the ungodly are finally consumed.

timeline.title: Gregory of Nyssa on restoration
timeline.note: Gregory describes judgment as a refining fire leading to universal thanksgiving.

timeline.title: Augustine, City of God Book 21
timeline.note: Augustine defends endless punishment against 'the merciful' and sets the Western norm.

timeline.title: Justinian's edict against Origen
timeline.note: The emperor condemns Origenist teachings, including claims about the eventual end of punishment.

timeline.title: Second Council of Constantinople and the anti-Origenist anathemas
timeline.note: Fifteen anathemas against Origenist doctrines are associated with the council. Historians debate whether they were formally adopted by the council itself and whether they condemned universal restoration as such or the specific Origenist cosmology of pre-existent minds.

timeline.title: Fourth Lateran Council
timeline.note: Its creed speaks of perpetual punishment for the wicked with the devil.

timeline.title: Augsburg Confession article 17
timeline.note: Lutherans reject those who teach that the punishments of the condemned will end.

timeline.title: Edwards preaches 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'
timeline.note: Endless punishment becomes central to revival preaching.

timeline.title: Edward White's Life in Christ
timeline.note: A major nineteenth-century statement of conditional immortality.

timeline.title: MacDonald's first Unspoken Sermons
timeline.note: MacDonald presents God's consuming fire as purifying love.

timeline.title: Fudge's The Fire That Consumes
timeline.note: A comprehensive evangelical case for conditionalism.

timeline.title: Stott's tentative annihilationism
timeline.note: In *Evangelical Essentials* Stott cautiously favors final annihilation, opening the evangelical debate.

timeline.title: Hart's That All Shall Be Saved
timeline.note: A high-profile philosophical and theological argument for universal salvation.

influence.note: Gregory adapted Origen's restoration hope while dropping some of his speculative cosmology.
Aquinas systematized Augustine's case for endless punishment.
Edwards inherited the Augustinian-Reformed account of sin and justice.
Hart draws heavily on Gregory's metaphysics of the Good.
Parry's pseudonym 'Gregory MacDonald' honors Gregory of Nyssa and George MacDonald.
Talbott cites MacDonald as a formative influence.
Rethinking Hell built on Fudge's exegetical case and honored him in an edited volume.
Stott's 1988 remarks gave Fudge's arguments wider evangelical hearing.

argumentMap.text: The lost suffer consciously and without end.
Matt 25:46 parallels eternal punishment with eternal life.
Revelation describes torment day and night for ever and ever.
Aiōnios can describe a permanent result rather than an endless process.
'Punishment' (kolasis) implies a subject undergoing it, not merely an outcome.
Rev 14:11 borrows Isa 34's imagery of a destroyed city whose smoke rises forever.
The lost are finally destroyed; immortality is God's gift in Christ.
God alone has immortality and gives it to those who seek it.
The lake of fire is called the second death.
The devil is tormented forever in the same lake, so it cannot simply annihilate.
The beast and false prophet are symbols of powers; for humans John explicitly defines the lake as death.
God will reconcile all people to himself through Christ.
Paul's Adam-Christ parallels make the scope of life as wide as the scope of death.
All things are reconciled and God becomes all in all.
Context limits the 'all' to those who receive grace and belong to Christ.
Universalists agree only those in Christ are saved; they argue all will eventually be in Christ.
Reconciliation can be achieved by removing rebels rather than converting them.
Endless punishment for finite sin is disproportionate.
Guilt is measured by the dignity of the one offended, and the lost continue in rebellion.
Constantinople 553 condemned apokatastasis.
Whether the anathemas were conciliar and whether they target restoration as such or Origenist cosmology is debated.

title: Heaven or New Creation?
question: Where is our final hope — heaven or a renewed earth?
intro:
Christians confess 'the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting', but they have pictured that life in different ways. One long tradition centers the final hope on heaven: the soul's ascent to God and the beatific vision, the direct sight of God that is humanity's supreme happiness. Another stresses that the Bible ends not with souls leaving earth but with God coming to dwell with his people in a renewed creation, raised bodies and all. A third, found in the Reformed and wider Protestant confessions, holds the two together in sequence: at death believers go to be with Christ in heaven, and at his return they are raised to live forever on a new earth.

These positions overlap more than popular debate suggests. Nearly everyone affirms bodily resurrection, and most new-creation writers affirm a conscious intermediate state. The real differences lie in emphasis and in specific questions: Is the vision of God or the renewal of creation the center of the final hope? Will the present world be renewed or replaced? How much continuity is there between present culture and the world to come? Is it right to speak of 'going to heaven' as the goal of salvation?

positions.name: Heaven as the destination (beatific vision)
positions.summary: The final goal of human life is God himself, enjoyed in the direct vision of his essence in heaven. Believers' souls go to be with God at death and, after the resurrection, glorified saints dwell with him forever in the heavenly realm. Material creation is not despised, but it is secondary: what the redeemed finally receive is not a place but a Person, seen face to face.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop of Hippo Regius; theologian
figures.bio: Augustine closes *City of God* with the eternal sabbath of the saints, whose final happiness is to see God, love him and praise him without end. He affirmed bodily resurrection, but the heart of his eschatology is restful contemplation of God, which shaped Western piety for a millennium.

figures.name: Thomas Aquinas
figures.profession: Dominican friar and theologian
figures.bio: Aquinas argued that human happiness can consist only in the vision of the divine essence, since nothing created can satisfy the intellect's desire to know the first cause. He taught bodily resurrection and a renewal of the heavens and earth, but viewed the renewed world chiefly as a fitting setting for glorified humans rather than as a sphere of ongoing activity.

works.author: Thomas Aquinas (compiled by Reginald of Piperno)
works.title: Summa Theologiae, Supplement

figures.name: Richard Baxter
figures.profession: English Puritan pastor at Kidderminster
figures.bio: Baxter wrote *The Saints' Everlasting Rest* while seriously ill, urging Christians to meditate daily on heavenly glory as the remedy for worldliness and the source of joy in suffering. It became one of the most widely read Puritan devotional books.

figures.name: Hans Boersma
figures.profession: Reformed-turned-Anglican theologian; professor at Nashotah House
figures.bio: Boersma traces the beatific vision through the Fathers, medieval and Reformed writers, arguing that seeing God in Christ is the true end of humanity and criticizing modern eschatologies that make the renewed creation, rather than God, the center of hope.

works.author: Hans Boersma
works.title: Seeing God: The Beatific Vision in Christian Tradition

figures.name: Michael Allen
figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology, Reformed Theological Seminary (Orlando)
figures.bio: Allen affirms the new creation but warns against what he calls an 'eschatological naturalism' that celebrates renewed earth and culture while losing sight of God himself as the goal. He calls for a recovery of heavenly-mindedness, self-denial and the beatific vision in Protestant theology.

works.author: Michael Allen
works.title: Grounded in Heaven: Recentering Christian Hope and Life on God

positions.context:
From Augustine through the medieval period, Christian hope was described above all as seeing God. Pope Benedict XII's constitution *Benedictus Deus* (1336) defined that the souls of the purified see the divine essence immediately after death, before the resurrection. Protestant piety kept the heavenly focus: Puritan meditation on heaven, Bunyan's Celestial City, and countless hymns about crossing over Jordan to the heavenly home. Some seventeenth-century Lutheran theologians taught that the present world would be annihilated rather than renewed.

In modern popular evangelicalism, 'going to heaven when you die' became the standard shorthand for salvation. Recent defenders such as Boersma and Allen are not defending a disembodied or world-denying hope; they generally affirm the resurrection and new creation. Their claim is about priority: God, seen and enjoyed, is the end, and creation matters as the medium of that communion.
claims: The ultimate end of human beings is God himself, seen and enjoyed directly (the beatific vision).
Heaven is where God's glory is fully present; the redeemed are destined to be with him there.
Believers enter heaven at death and enjoy God's presence immediately.
The resurrection body is real but spiritual and glorified, suited to heavenly life.
Earthly goods are signs pointing beyond themselves; fixing hope on them risks idolatry.
Christian life should be shaped by heavenly-mindedness and longing for God.

scriptures.reading: Jesus goes to prepare a place in the Father's house and will take his disciples to be where he is: the destination is with Christ in the Father's dwelling.
To depart and be with Christ is 'far better'; heaven at death is a genuine and desirable goal.
Believers have a building from God, eternal in the heavens, and prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
The patriarchs were strangers on earth seeking a better, heavenly country, and God has prepared a city for them.
Christians are to seek the things above where Christ is, not things on earth.
The inheritance is imperishable and kept in heaven.
We shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is: the vision of God transforms.
The pure in heart will see God: the beatitude of beatitudes.
Even in the new Jerusalem the climax is that 'they will see his face'.

arguments.text: The New Testament repeatedly locates the believer's reward, citizenship and inheritance in heaven.
The climax of every biblical description of final blessing is seeing God, not enjoying a place.
Only an infinite good can satisfy a creature made for God; created goods, however renewed, cannot be the final end.
If the final hope is a renewed version of present goods, the Christian life risks becoming an improved worldliness rather than self-denial and love of God.
The beatific vision has been the shared center of patristic, medieval, Reformation and Puritan eschatology; the modern shift away from it is recent.
The Church's martyrs and ascetics drew strength from hope of heavenly glory, showing the spiritual fruitfulness of this emphasis.

critiques.text: The Bible's final scene is not souls going up but the new Jerusalem coming down; making heaven the destination imports a Platonic contrast between spirit and matter that sidelines bodily resurrection and creation's renewal.
Texts like John 14:2-3 and Phil 1:23 describe being with Christ, not leaving creation; 'heaven' in many New Testament texts is where future realities are kept until they are revealed on earth.
Collapsing the intermediate state and the final state into one 'heaven' obscures the biblical sequence: the souls under the altar still await the resurrection and the renewal of all things.

responses.text: Classical defenders affirm bodily resurrection and new creation; the point is that even in Rev 21–22 the center is God's presence and the vision of his face. Seeking God above all is biblical, not Platonic.

Even if heaven is where future realities are kept, the New Testament genuinely calls believers to set their minds on things above and to long to be with Christ; that orientation should not be lost in emphasis on earthly renewal.

The sequence is accepted; what matters is that the same reality, communion with God in Christ, begins at death and is perfected at the resurrection. 'Heaven' rightly names that reality at both stages.

strawMen.strawMan: This view teaches that we become disembodied spirits floating on clouds playing harps forever.
strawMen.correction: Its theological defenders affirm bodily resurrection; cloud-and-harp images come from popular culture, not from Augustine, Aquinas or the Puritans.

strawMen.strawMan: It holds that the material world is evil and will be thrown away.
strawMen.correction: Most classical writers affirmed the goodness and renewal of creation; their claim is that creation is not the final end, God is.

strawMen.strawMan: Heavenly-mindedness makes Christians indifferent to justice and culture.
strawMen.correction: Defenders argue that hope fixed on God frees people from idolatry of earthly goods and has historically motivated sacrificial service.

positive: Keeps God himself, rather than his gifts, at the center of hope and worship.
Provides deep consolation to the dying and bereaved.
Nourishes contemplative prayer and detachment from consumerism.
negative: In popular forms it has encouraged an escapist view of salvation and neglect of the body and creation.
It can make bodily resurrection seem an afterthought.
'Going to heaven' language can obscure the biblical storyline of creation's renewal.

adherents: Classical Roman Catholic theology (Benedictus Deus; Catechism §1023–1029)
Much medieval and Puritan devotional tradition
Popular evangelical and revivalist piety and hymnody
Contemporary retrievers of the beatific vision (Hans Boersma, Michael Allen)

proponent.author: Hans Boersma
proponent.title: Seeing God: The Beatific Vision in Christian Tradition

critic.author: J. Richard Middleton
critic.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth

sequence: At death the believer's soul, purified, goes to be with God in heaven and begins to see him.
The body lies in the grave awaiting resurrection.
At Christ's return the dead are raised in glorified, spiritual bodies.
After the last judgment the redeemed dwell with God in heavenly glory; the material world is renewed as a setting or, in some older views, passes away.
The saints' eternal activity is seeing, loving and praising God: the beatific vision.

positions.name: New creation (resurrection and renewed earth)
positions.summary: The Christian hope is not escaping to heaven but the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the whole creation, when heaven and earth are joined and God dwells with his people. Heaven at death is a real but temporary rest; the final destination is a transformed earth where redeemed humans live, worship, work and reign with Christ.

figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
figures.profession: Bishop of Lyon; anti-Gnostic theologian
figures.bio: Against Gnostics who despised matter, Irenaeus insisted that God would redeem the very creation in which the righteous had suffered. In the final chapters of *Against Heresies* he argues that the promises to Abraham of land must be fulfilled in a renewed earth, that creation will be restored to its original state, and that the righteous will reign in it.

figures.name: Jürgen Moltmann
figures.profession: German Reformed theologian, University of Tübingen
figures.bio: Moltmann's 'theology of hope' made eschatology the horizon of all theology. In *The Coming of God* he describes the final future as the cosmic indwelling of God in a new creation, rejecting a merely individual or heavenly hope.

works.author: Jürgen Moltmann
works.title: The Coming of God: Christian Eschatology

figures.name: N. T. Wright
figures.profession: New Testament scholar; former Anglican Bishop of Durham
figures.bio: Wright argues that first-century Jews and early Christians hoped for bodily resurrection within a renewed world, and that 'going to heaven' is at most a temporary stage, 'life after death' followed by 'life after life after death'. He urges churches to recover the earthy hope of Rev 21–22 and its implications for justice, beauty and mission now.

works.author: N. T. Wright
works.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God

figures.name: J. Richard Middleton
figures.profession: Professor of biblical worldview and exegesis, Northeastern Seminary
figures.bio: Middleton traces a 'holistic eschatology' across the canon, from humanity's earthly vocation in Genesis through the prophets to Rev 21–22. He argues that 2 Pet 3 describes purging and disclosure, not annihilation, and that 'heaven' was never meant to be the final home of the redeemed.

works.author: J. Richard Middleton
works.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth: Reclaiming Biblical Eschatology

figures.name: Randy Alcorn
figures.profession: American evangelical author and pastor
figures.bio: Alcorn's best-selling *Heaven* brought new-earth eschatology to a broad evangelical readership, using the word 'heaven' but arguing at length that the eternal home of believers is a physical, renewed earth with culture, work and relationships.

positions.context:
Second-century writers such as Irenaeus and Justin Martyr expected a renewed earth, often bound up with a millennial reign. As allegorical and Platonic currents grew and chiliasm fell out of favor, the earthly dimension of hope receded in much of Christian thought, though it was never wholly lost. Reformed theology (Calvin, Kuyper, Bavinck) emphasized creation's renewal.

In the twentieth century, biblical theology's recovery of the Jewish background of resurrection, and theologians such as Moltmann, revived interest in cosmic renewal. N. T. Wright's *Surprised by Hope* (2008) and Middleton's *A New Heaven and a New Earth* (2014) made the new-creation emphasis widely known, influencing evangelical, Anglican and Catholic preaching, creation care and theology of work. Its defenders do not deny the intermediate state; they deny that it is the goal.
claims: The final hope is bodily resurrection in a renewed, physical creation.
God will not discard the world but liberate it from corruption, as he raised Jesus' body.
Heaven and earth will be united; God will dwell with humans on earth.
The intermediate state with Christ is real but temporary.
Redeemed humans will resume their vocation to steward and rule creation under God.
Work done 'in the Lord' now has lasting significance in the new creation.

scriptures.reading: Creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay when God's children receive the redemption of their bodies.
The new Jerusalem comes down out of heaven and God's dwelling is with humans; God says he makes all things new, not all new things.
The new heavens and new earth include houses, vineyards, long life and peace among animals: a renewed world, not an ethereal one.
Believers wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells.
Heaven receives Jesus only until the time for restoring all things spoken of by the prophets.
Jesus speaks of the 'renewal' (palingenesia) of all things, when the apostles share his rule.
The meek will inherit the earth.
Our citizenship is in heaven, and from heaven we await a Savior who will transform our bodies: heaven is the source, not the destination.
The redeemed are made a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth.
Christ's bodily resurrection is the firstfruits of the harvest of the redeemed creation.

arguments.text: The biblical storyline begins with humans placed on earth to rule it and ends with God's dwelling coming down to earth; the final scenes of Revelation are earthy, urban and bodily.
Jesus' resurrection body, which could be touched and could eat, is the pattern for the redeemed and shows that God redeems matter rather than discarding it.

In 2 Pet 3:10 the earliest manuscripts read that the earth and its works 'will be found' or laid bare, not 'burned up', suggesting purification and disclosure rather than annihilation; the flood analogy in 3:6 describes a cleansed world, not a destroyed one.
If God abandoned the material world, the devil's corruption of creation would have the last word; redemption must be as wide as the fall.
Second Temple Jewish hope, which Jesus and Paul shared, was resurrection within a renewed world, not disembodied bliss.
The earliest post-apostolic writers, notably Irenaeus, expected creation's renewal; the later heavenly emphasis reflects the growing influence of Platonism.

critiques.text: By focusing on renewed earth, culture and vocation, the view risks making the final hope a perfected world rather than God himself, an 'eschatological naturalism' that sidelines the beatific vision.
It downplays the many texts that direct hope to heaven and the real discontinuity between this age and the next, including texts on the passing away of the present heavens and earth.
Popular new-creation rhetoric sometimes speaks dismissively of heaven, slighting the real and blessed intermediate state that comforted Paul and the martyrs.

responses.text: Rev 21–22 places the vision of God's face at the center of the renewed city; new creation is the setting in which God is seen and enjoyed, not a rival to him. Loving God through his renewed gifts is not idolatry.

Heaven in the New Testament is where future blessings are kept and from where they come; 'passing away' language describes transformation of the present order, as the old body passes into the new without ceasing to be the same person.
Leading new-creation writers explicitly affirm the intermediate state as being with Christ and 'far better'; they object only to making it the final goal.

strawMen.strawMan: New-creation advocates deny heaven or deny that believers go to be with Christ at death.
strawMen.correction: Wright, Middleton and Alcorn affirm the intermediate state; they argue it is a temporary stage before resurrection.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a social-gospel program that thinks humans will build the kingdom by their own efforts.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders say the new creation is God's act at Christ's return; human work matters because God will take it up, not because it builds the kingdom unaided.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a modern invention driven by environmentalism.
strawMen.correction: Its core claims appear in Irenaeus and Reformed dogmatics long before modern environmental movements.

positive: Restores the centrality of bodily resurrection and the goodness of creation.
Grounds creation care, justice and the dignity of ordinary work.
Gives a coherent reading of the Bible's storyline from Genesis to Revelation.
negative: Can slide into an immanent, this-worldly hope with little sense of God's transcendence.
Popular versions sometimes caricature traditional piety and the comfort of heaven.
Speculation about life on the new earth can outrun what Scripture says.

adherents: Many contemporary evangelical and Anglican scholars and preachers
Neo-Calvinist (Kuyperian) Reformed circles
Much contemporary biblical theology
Creation-care and faith-and-work movements

proponent.author: J. Richard Middleton
proponent.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth

critic.author: Michael Horton
critic.title: The Christian Faith: A Systematic Theology for Pilgrims on the Way

sequence: At death the believer rests consciously with Christ: 'life after death', a real but temporary stage.
At Christ's return the dead are raised in transformed, physical bodies like his.
Judgment sets the world right; creation is freed from decay and purified, not discarded.
Heaven and earth are joined; the new Jerusalem descends and God dwells with humanity.
The redeemed reign with Christ, worship God face to face, and carry out renewed human vocation on the new earth forever.

positions.name: Intermediate state, then new creation (two-stage confessional view)
positions.summary: Christian hope has two stages, both essential. At death believers' souls are made perfect and go immediately to be with Christ in heaven, a conscious and blessed state; at Christ's return they are raised bodily and live forever on a renewed earth, where they will see God. Heaven is both the believer's present home after death and, as God's dwelling come down, a dimension of the final new creation.

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: French Reformer and pastor in Geneva
figures.bio: Calvin's first theological treatise argued against the idea that souls sleep between death and resurrection, defending conscious rest with Christ. In the *Institutes* he stresses that hope must look to the final resurrection, and he expected the renewal of creation.

figures.name: The Westminster Assembly
figures.profession: Assembly of English and Scottish divines
figures.bio: The Westminster Confession states that at death the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into the highest heavens, where they behold God's face while waiting for the full redemption of their bodies; at the last day the dead are raised with the same bodies. It became the doctrinal standard of Presbyterianism worldwide.

figures.name: Herman Bavinck
figures.profession: Dutch Reformed theologian, Kampen and Free University of Amsterdam
figures.bio: Bavinck taught that grace restores and perfects nature rather than abolishing it. His eschatology combines a blessed intermediate state with a renewed creation that is substantially continuous with the present world, while making the vision and enjoyment of God its crown.

works.author: Herman Bavinck
works.title: Reformed Dogmatics, vol. 4: Holy Spirit, Church, and New Creation

figures.name: Anthony A. Hoekema
figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology, Calvin Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Hoekema's *The Bible and the Future* treats the intermediate state and the new earth in one coherent scheme. He argued that the new earth is the renewal of this earth, that the cultural treasures of the nations will be taken into it, and that neglect of the new earth had impoverished evangelical eschatology.

figures.name: Michael Horton
figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology, Westminster Seminary California
figures.bio: Horton's systematic theology presents a covenantal eschatology in which believers enter Christ's presence at death and await the consummation of the whole creation at his return, with both stages integral to the one hope.

works.author: Michael Horton
works.title: The Christian Faith: A Systematic Theology for Pilgrims on the Way

positions.context:
The Reformers rejected purgatory and soul sleep and insisted that believers go immediately to Christ at death, while looking forward to the resurrection and the renewal of the world. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Q. 57–58), the Belgic Confession (1561, art. 37) and the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 32–33) all present this two-stage hope. Dutch neo-Calvinists (Kuyper, Bavinck) developed the theme of creation's renewal, and Hoekema brought it to a wide evangelical audience in 1979.

This view overlaps heavily with both other positions: it shares the classical emphasis on seeing God and the new-creation emphasis on the earth's renewal. Its distinctive contribution is to treat both stages as equally part of the gospel hope and to resist the tendency of either emphasis to slight the other. It is also the formal position of many Lutheran, Anglican and Baptist confessions, though their popular piety often emphasizes one stage.
claims: At death believers' souls are made perfect and immediately enter Christ's presence in heaven, consciously.
The intermediate state is blessed but incomplete; the dead in Christ still await the resurrection.
At Christ's return the same bodies are raised, glorified and reunited with souls.
The present creation will be renewed and purified, not annihilated and replaced.
In the final state God's dwelling is with humanity on the new earth, and the redeemed see God's face.
Both the vision of God and the renewal of creation belong to the one Christian hope.

scriptures.reading: Jesus promises the penitent thief that he will be with him in paradise that day: immediate presence with Christ at death.
To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better, yet Paul elsewhere longs for the resurrection: a real but interim blessing.
Paul prefers to be at home with the Lord, though he does not want to be 'unclothed' but further clothed: the intermediate state is good, the resurrection better.
The heavenly Jerusalem already includes 'the spirits of the righteous made perfect'.
The souls of martyrs are conscious, rest, and still wait for final justice.
Those who have fallen asleep in Jesus come with him and are raised when he returns.
What is sown perishable is raised imperishable: the same body transformed.
Creation awaits liberation together with the redemption of our bodies.
The new heaven and earth are the final home where God dwells with his people.
In the renewed city the servants of God see his face and reign forever.

arguments.text: The New Testament teaches both an immediate presence with Christ at death and a future bodily resurrection; any account that drops either is incomplete.
Paul's language of being 'unclothed' and 'further clothed' shows the intermediate state is real yet not the goal.
Revelation pictures heaven both now (the throne room, the souls under the altar) and as coming down to a new earth at the end.
Personal identity through death and resurrection requires a continuing conscious self, which the intermediate state provides.
If God renews rather than replaces the body, consistency suggests he renews rather than replaces creation.
The two-stage hope is the formal teaching of the major Reformation confessions and has the broadest confessional backing among Protestants.

critiques.text: Treating the intermediate state as merely interim risks diminishing the reality that believers already see God at death; the vision of God, not a renewed earth, is what makes the final state final.

The language of souls being 'received into the highest heavens' leans on a body-soul dualism that the Hebrew Bible does not clearly teach; the intermediate state is described too sparingly in Scripture to build much on.
In practice the confessional view has often functioned as heaven-centered piety with the new earth as an appendix, so it has not prevented the problems it claims to avoid.

responses.text: The confessions say the departed already behold God's face (WCF 32.1); the resurrection does not add a better God but a fuller humanity to see him with.
Jesus himself speaks of killing the body but not the soul, and promises paradise 'today'; a modest body-soul distinction is biblical, while affirming that the person is meant to be embodied.
That is a failure of teaching, not of the doctrine; Hoekema and Bavinck gave the new earth full weight within the confessional framework.

strawMen.strawMan: This is just a compromise that splits the difference without a principle.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders argue the two stages arise directly from distinct sets of texts and are both affirmed in the earliest Reformation confessions.

strawMen.strawMan: It teaches that heaven is a waiting room where nothing good happens.
strawMen.correction: It describes the intermediate state as perfect holiness and communion with Christ, 'far better' than now, though not yet the fullness of resurrection.

strawMen.strawMan: It is identical to the popular 'go to heaven when you die' view.
strawMen.correction: It explicitly makes the bodily resurrection and renewed creation the final state, which many popular forms omit.

positive: Gives pastoral comfort at death while keeping the resurrection central.
Integrates the vision of God and the renewal of creation in one hope.
Provides a stable confessional framework across many denominations.
negative: Its balance is often lost in practice, tilting toward one stage.
Requires a body-soul distinction that some biblical scholars question.
Details of the intermediate state remain largely unspecified, inviting speculation.

adherents: Presbyterian and Reformed churches (Westminster Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Belgic Confession)
Many Lutheran, Anglican and Baptist confessional statements
Dutch neo-Calvinist tradition
Many evangelical systematic theologians

sequence: At death the believer's body returns to the dust but remains united to Christ; the soul is made perfect in holiness.
The soul passes immediately into Christ's presence in heaven, conscious and at rest, beholding God while awaiting the resurrection.
At Christ's return the dead are raised with the same bodies, transformed and glorified, and reunited with their souls.
The last judgment publicly acquits believers; creation is purified and renewed.
God's dwelling comes to the new earth; the redeemed see his face and live, worship and reign there forever.

readings.reading: The Father's house with many rooms is heaven, and Jesus will take his followers there to be with him.
The 'rooms' (monai) are dwellings or stopping places; the stress is on being with Jesus, and in John the Father's house becomes the place where God dwells with people (John 14:23).
The promise is fulfilled in stages: believers are with Christ at death, and he comes again to bring them into the final dwelling of God.
Being with Christ in heaven is 'far better' and is the Christian's desire.
It is better than life now but not the final hope; in Phil 3:20-21 Paul's hope is the bodily transformation at Christ's coming.
The verse teaches a conscious, blessed intermediate state that is real but penultimate.
Away from the body is at home with the Lord: heavenly presence is the goal.
Paul prefers to be 'further clothed' (5:4), not unclothed; being away from the body is the lesser good he accepts.
Being at home with the Lord is the intermediate state, preferable to life now yet awaiting the resurrection body.
The patriarchs sought a heavenly country, not the earthly Canaan.
'Heavenly' describes the origin and quality of the city God prepares, the city that in Rev 21 comes down to earth.
The heavenly city is now in heaven and will be revealed on the new earth at the end.
Creation shares in redemption as the setting for glorified humanity, but the focus is the revealing of the children of God.
Creation itself is set free from decay; the cosmos is redeemed, not discarded.
The redemption of our bodies and the liberation of creation happen together at the final stage.
The new Jerusalem is the glorified heavenly realm in which God's presence fills everything.
The city comes down out of heaven to the new earth: God moves in with humanity, not humanity out of the world.
This is the final stage, after the intermediate state, when heaven's life arrives on a renewed earth.
The present heavens and earth pass away with fire; believers look beyond this world, and some older theologians took this as annihilation.
The best manuscripts read that the earth 'will be found' (laid bare); the fire purifies, as the flood cleansed the world.
The fire is a purging judgment that renews rather than replaces the creation, yielding a new earth where righteousness dwells.
Seeing God as he is, and being transformed by that sight, is the heart of the final hope.
The seeing happens 'when he appears', at his coming, which is the moment of resurrection and renewal.
The vision of God begins for souls after death and is completed in the resurrection when we are fully like him.

timeline.note: Puritan classic of heavenly meditation.
