influence.note: Aquinas developed Augustine's vision of rest in God into a theory of the beatific vision.
Boersma retrieves the scholastic and patristic vision of God.
Middleton appeals to Irenaeus as an early holistic eschatology.
The confession's two-stage hope follows Calvin's teaching.
Hoekema's new-earth emphasis draws on the Dutch Reformed tradition.
Alcorn draws on Hoekema's treatment of the new earth.
Both helped shift twentieth-century eschatology toward cosmic renewal, though Wright works mainly from historical exegesis.

argumentMap.text: The final end of human beings is the vision of God in heaven.
Every biblical climax of blessing is seeing God.
Reward, citizenship and inheritance are located in heaven.
Heaven is where future realities are kept until revealed on earth; Christ comes from heaven to transform us.
Even so, Christians are commanded to set their minds above and to long for Christ's presence.
The final hope is resurrection on a renewed earth where God dwells with humanity.
The new Jerusalem comes down; God's dwelling is with humans.
Creation itself will be freed from decay.
2 Pet 3:10's earliest reading points to purification, not annihilation.
Making renewed creation the center risks eschatological naturalism that forgets God himself.
The renewed city's center is the throne and the face of God.
Hope has two stages: with Christ at death, resurrection on the new earth at his return.
Paradise today and being with Christ at death are promised.
The martyrs under the altar are conscious and still waiting.
The body-soul dualism of the confessions goes beyond what the Hebrew Bible teaches.
Jesus distinguishes body and soul and promises presence with him that day.
Treating heaven after death as merely interim diminishes the vision of God already given.
The confessions say the departed already behold God's face; resurrection adds fuller humanity, not a better God.
Popular new-creation rhetoric dismisses the blessed intermediate state.
Leading new-creation scholars affirm the intermediate state; they deny only that it is final.

title: Jesus as the Lens for Scripture
question: Is Jesus the lens through which to read the whole Bible, including OT violence?
intro:
All Christians read the Bible as pointing to Christ, but they disagree about what that means when an Old Testament text seems to portray God very differently from Jesus, above all in the commands to destroy the Canaanites (Deut 7; Deut 20; 1 Sam 15). Some argue that Jesus, and especially his crucifixion, is the full revelation of God's character, so that any portrait of God that conflicts with the cross must be reinterpreted in its light (a christocentric or cruciform hermeneutic). Others hold that every part of Scripture reveals God's character directly, that divine judgment is just and consistent across both Testaments, and that the New Testament itself portrays Christ as judge (a whole-canon reading, sometimes called 'flat' by its critics). A middle view reads the canon toward Christ as its goal and climax, so that the Old Testament is reread in his light, but without letting Christ overrule or cancel what the Old Testament says.

The debate raises old questions. In the second century Marcion rejected the Old Testament's God as a lesser deity; the church rejected Marcion and affirmed one God of both Testaments. Critics argue that some christocentric readings drift toward a functional Marcionism; their defenders reply that they keep the whole Old Testament as inspired Scripture. The other positions face their own challenges: how to read genocide commands as revelation of a good God, and how to keep christological rereading from becoming arbitrary.

positions.name: Christocentric-cruciform hermeneutic
positions.summary: Jesus, and supremely the crucified Jesus, is the full and final revelation of God's character. All Scripture is inspired, but its portraits of God are to be read through the cross: where an Old Testament text depicts God commanding violence that conflicts with the self-giving love revealed in Christ, the text reflects the limited perspective of its human authors, or God's accommodation to them, rather than God's true character.

figures.name: Origen of Alexandria
figures.profession: Alexandrian biblical scholar and theologian
figures.bio: Origen read Joshua's wars as figures of the Christian's spiritual battle against sin and demonic powers, arguing that a literal reading unworthy of God signaled a deeper spiritual sense. Modern cruciform writers cite him as a precedent for refusing to take violent portraits of God at face value, though his method was allegorical rather than a theology of accommodation.

figures.name: Gregory A. Boyd
figures.profession: Senior pastor of Woodland Hills Church (St. Paul, Minnesota); theologian
figures.bio: Boyd's two-volume *Crucifixion of the Warrior God* argues that the cross is the lens through which all Scripture's portraits of God must be read. He holds that the Old Testament's violent portraits are inspired, but that God inspired them by humbly allowing his people to depict him according to their fallen, culturally conditioned expectations, just as on the cross he bore the appearance of a guilty criminal. He also argues that judgments in Scripture often occur as God withdraws and allows sin's self-destructive consequences.

works.author: Gregory A. Boyd
works.title: The Crucifixion of the Warrior God (2 vols.)

works.author: Gregory A. Boyd
works.title: Cross Vision: How the Crucifixion of Jesus Makes Sense of Old Testament Violence

figures.name: Brian Zahnd
figures.profession: Founding pastor of Word of Life Church, St. Joseph, Missouri
figures.bio: Zahnd, once a charismatic megachurch pastor, became a widely read advocate of a Christ-shaped, nonviolent picture of God. He argues that God is like Jesus and has always been like Jesus, and that the Bible is a progressive witness culminating in Christ.

works.author: Brian Zahnd
works.title: Sinners in the Hands of a Loving God

figures.name: Bill Johnson
figures.profession: Senior leader of Bethel Church, Redding, California
figures.bio: Johnson popularized the phrase 'Jesus Christ is perfect theology', meaning that Jesus' life is the clearest picture of God's will. He uses it mainly in arguing for divine healing (Jesus healed all who came to him, so sickness is not God's will) rather than in debates about Old Testament violence, but the slogan has been widely taken up as shorthand for christocentric reading.

works.author: Bill Johnson
works.title: Sermons and writings using the phrase 'Jesus Christ is perfect theology'

figures.name: Peter Enns
figures.profession: Biblical scholar, Eastern University
figures.bio: Enns used the term 'christotelic' for apostolic interpretation that reads Israel's story in light of its goal in Christ rather than finding Christ on the surface of every text. In later work he argues that the Old Testament's violent portraits reflect how ancient Israelites understood God in their tribal setting, and that Jesus provides the decisive correction.

positions.context:
Christ-centered reading is as old as the New Testament, but the specific move of letting Christ's nonviolence reinterpret violent portraits of God has ancient and modern roots. Origen allegorized the conquest. Luther judged books by whether they 'promote Christ'. Twentieth-century theologians such as Karl Barth made Christ the center of all doctrine, and Anabaptist and Mennonite traditions read Scripture through the Sermon on the Mount.

The contemporary cruciform hermeneutic grew from these streams alongside the post-9/11 debate over religion and violence and the 'New Atheist' attack on Old Testament violence. Eric Seibert's *Disturbing Divine Behavior* (2009), Derek Flood's *Disarming Scripture* (2014), Enns, Zahnd and above all Boyd's 2017 work gave it shape. Its defenders insist they are not Marcionites: they keep the whole Old Testament as inspired, and they read it as testimony that, rightly interpreted, points to the crucified God.
claims: Jesus is the full and final revelation of God; no prior revelation is equal to him.
The cross is the clearest expression of who God is: self-giving, enemy-loving love.
All Scripture is inspired, but not every portrait of God within it shows his true character directly.
Violent portraits of God reflect his accommodation to his people's fallen understanding, or the human authors' limited view.
Divine judgment is real, but it usually takes the form of God withdrawing and letting sin destroy itself.
Christians should imitate the God revealed in Jesus, which rules out violence done in God's name.

scriptures.reading: God spoke in many partial ways through the prophets, but now in a Son who is the exact imprint of his nature: the Son is the standard for all earlier revelation.
No one has ever seen God; the Son has made him known. Earlier portraits were not full sight of God.
Whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father; there is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him.
Christ is the image of the invisible God.
The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ.

When the disciples propose calling down fire like Elijah, Jesus rebukes them, rejecting a precedent drawn from the Old Testament. (The words about 'what spirit you are of' in v. 55-56 are absent from many early manuscripts.)
Jesus revises 'eye for eye' and commands love of enemies precisely so that his followers will be like their Father.
God's glory is seen in the face of Jesus Christ.
Paul resolves to know nothing but Christ crucified: the cross is the center of revelation.

arguments.text: The New Testament says explicitly that Jesus surpasses earlier revelation and is the exact representation of God's being.
Jesus himself corrected Old Testament precedents and laws, showing that not every earlier text expresses God's ideal will.
The Old Testament already contains counter-testimony to violent portraits, such as Hosea's refusal to come in wrath and Ezekiel's statement that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
If God is perfectly revealed in the crucified Christ who prays for his enemies, he cannot also be a God who commands the killing of infants; one of these portraits must be read in light of the other.

The cross shows God willing to bear an ugly, distorted appearance for the sake of others; the violent portraits can be understood the same way, as God bearing his people's sin by letting them depict him wrongly.
Early Christian writers such as Origen recognized that some Old Testament depictions were unworthy of God if read literally, and reread them spiritually.

critiques.text: Setting Christ against the Old Testament's portraits of God drifts toward Marcionism, the second-century heresy that separated the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus. Even if the Old Testament is formally retained, its voice is muted wherever it disagrees with the interpreter's picture of Jesus.

The Jesus of the New Testament is also a judge: he speaks of Gehenna, overturns tables, and in Revelation strikes the nations; the New Testament records God's lethal judgment (Ananias and Sapphira). A cruciform filter selects a Jesus who is less than the canonical one.

Jesus and the apostles never treat Old Testament portraits of God as distortions; they read them as true witness pointing to him. Treating texts as God's 'accommodation' to false views risks making the interpreter's moral intuitions the real authority.

responses.text: Marcion rejected the Old Testament and its God; cruciform readers affirm one God of both Testaments and the inspiration of every text. They claim not that the God of Israel is another God, but that the same God is fully revealed only in Christ, which the Old Testament itself anticipates.

Boyd and others affirm judgment but interpret it through the cross: God judges by withdrawing protection and letting sin's consequences fall, as Paul describes God 'handing over' sinners. Revelation's warrior Christ conquers by his own blood and the sword from his mouth, the word.
Jesus did treat some Old Testament provisions as concessions to hardness of heart. The cruciform approach extends that principle; its authority is the revealed Christ, not private intuition.

strawMen.strawMan: Cruciform readers simply throw out the parts of the Bible they don't like.
strawMen.correction: Boyd and most cruciform readers explicitly hold the whole canon to be inspired and argue that violent portraits have a revelatory function when read through the cross.

strawMen.strawMan: They believe God never judges anyone.
strawMen.correction: Most affirm real divine judgment; they dispute its mode, holding that God judges chiefly by allowing sin to run its destructive course.

strawMen.strawMan: 'Jesus is perfect theology' means only the red letters matter.
strawMen.correction: The phrase claims that Jesus' whole person and work reveals God fully; it is not a rule that only his recorded words count.

positive: Keeps the character of Jesus central to the Christian doctrine of God.
Offers a way through Old Testament violence for those whose faith is troubled by it.
Strongly resists religious justifications of violence and warfare.
negative: Risks a functional Marcionism in which the Old Testament loses its authority.
Can underplay divine holiness and judgment that the New Testament also teaches.
Interpreters may select an image of Jesus that suits modern sensibilities.

adherents: Anabaptist and Mennonite theologians (in various forms)
Progressive evangelical and post-evangelical writers
ReKnew (Greg Boyd's ministry) and Woodland Hills Church
Some charismatic leaders who use the 'Jesus is perfect theology' slogan

proponent.author: Eric A. Seibert
proponent.title: Disturbing Divine Behavior: Troubling Old Testament Images of God

proponent.author: Brian Zahnd
proponent.title: Sinners in the Hands of a Loving God

sequence: Begin with Jesus, especially the cross, as the full revelation of God's character.
Read a violent Old Testament portrait of God (e.g. 1 Sam 15) as inspired testimony, not as a direct snapshot of God's will.
Ask how the portrait reflects the human author's fallen or culturally conditioned understanding that God accommodated.
Look for the 'cross-like' meaning: God bearing his people's distorted picture of him, and judgment occurring as he withdraws and sin destroys itself.
Apply the same lens to final judgment: the lost experience the consequences of rejecting self-giving love, not a God unlike Jesus.
Conclude with imitation: Christians reject violence in God's name and love enemies as Jesus did.

positions.name: Whole-canon reading (divine judgment as just)
positions.summary: Every part of Scripture is God's word and reveals his character truly, though not every part reveals it equally fully. The God who commanded judgment on the Canaanites is the same God revealed in Jesus, and that judgment was just: a response to long-standing, grievous sin, limited in scope, and a foreshadowing of the final judgment that Jesus himself will carry out. The cross does not cancel divine wrath; it is where wrath and mercy meet.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop of Hippo; former Manichee
figures.bio: Responding to the Manichean Faustus, who claimed the Old Testament God was unworthy of Christ, Augustine defended the patriarchs and Israel's wars as acts of a just God. He argued that the real evils in war are cruelty and lust for domination, not the death of those who would die anyway, and that God may justly command war as punishment.

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: Reformer and pastor in Geneva
figures.bio: In his commentary on Joshua, Calvin acknowledged that the slaughter of women and children seems at first sight cruel, but insisted that God's command must be accepted as just because God is the judge of all, and that the Canaanites' iniquity had reached its full measure.

figures.name: Paul Copan
figures.profession: Philosopher of religion, Palm Beach Atlantic University
figures.bio: Copan argues that God really commanded the conquest, but that the commands use Ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric that is hyperbolic: 'utterly destroy' targeted military strongholds and meant decisive victory, not literal extermination of every person. He defends both the authority of the texts and their moral coherence with the rest of Scripture.

works.author: Paul Copan
works.title: Is God a Moral Monster? Making Sense of the Old Testament God

works.author: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan
works.title: Did God Really Command Genocide? Coming to Terms with the Justice of God

figures.name: Matthew Flannagan
figures.profession: New Zealand philosopher and Anglican priest
figures.bio: Flannagan co-authored the philosophical and exegetical defense of the conquest narratives with Copan, arguing in particular that divine command theory makes God's commands the standard of obligation and that the commands, rightly read, were not genocidal in the modern sense.

figures.name: Clay Jones
figures.profession: Apologist; associate professor at Talbot School of Theology (Biola University)
figures.bio: Jones argues that modern readers are troubled by the conquest because they underestimate the depravity of Canaanite practice (including child sacrifice and ritual sexual abuse) and the seriousness of sin generally. God's judgment on Canaan, he contends, was just and a warning of the universal judgment all sinners deserve.

works.author: Clay Jones
works.title: "We Don't Hate Sin So We Don't Understand What Happened to the Canaanites", Philosophia Christi 11:1

positions.context:
The label 'flat' is used mainly by critics; defenders describe their approach as reading the whole canon as God's word, recognizing progressive revelation but denying that later revelation corrects earlier revelation's picture of God. The view has deep roots: against Marcion and the Manichees, the church insisted that the God of Israel is the Father of Jesus and that his Old Testament acts were just. Augustine, Aquinas and the Reformers defended the conquest as a just judgment.

The modern debate intensified after the New Atheist critique (e.g. Richard Dawkins) and the cruciform proposals. Defenders differ in method: some (Copan, Flannagan) argue that the war texts are hyperbolic and less sweeping than they look; others (Jones, many Reformed theologians) accept a more literal reading and defend it as just judgment on a culture whose sin had become 'complete'. Tremper Longman's chapter in *Show Them No Mercy* (2003) traced a continuity from Israel's holy war to Christ's spiritual warfare and final judgment.
claims: All Scripture is God-breathed and reveals his character truly.
God's character does not change between the Testaments; the Father of Jesus is the God of Israel.
The conquest was a just judgment on persistent, grievous sin, not ethnic hatred.
Many 'utterly destroy' texts use stylized war rhetoric and should not be read as modern genocide.
The conquest was unique and unrepeatable, not a model for Christian violence.
The cross displays both God's love and his justice, satisfying wrath rather than abolishing it.
Jesus himself will judge the nations at the end.

scriptures.reading: God delays judgment on the Amorites for four centuries because their iniquity was not yet complete: the conquest was patient and just.
Israel receives the land not because of its righteousness but because of the nations' wickedness: judgment, not favoritism.
The land 'vomits out' its inhabitants for their practices, and would do the same to Israel.
The command is aimed at removing idolatry; the same chapter assumes Israel will not intermarry, suggesting the destruction language is not total extermination.
The command against Amalek recalls its unprovoked attacks on the vulnerable (Exod 17; Deut 25:17-19); it is judicial, not arbitrary.
God's righteousness is shown in the cross so that he is both just and the justifier: the cross upholds divine justice.
The returning Christ judges and makes war in righteousness: the New Testament's Jesus is also the warrior-judge.
'I the LORD do not change.'
All Scripture, which for Paul meant the Old Testament, is God-breathed and profitable.

arguments.text: The New Testament affirms the Old Testament's judgments as acts of God and uses them as warnings, not as misunderstandings to be corrected.
Jesus speaks more about final judgment than anyone else in the Bible, and the New Testament records God's direct lethal judgments.
The same narratives that command destruction also record mercy to Canaanites who turned to Israel's God, showing the issue was moral and religious, not ethnic.
As Creator and Judge of all, God has the right to take life; all humans are under a death sentence, and God may execute it at any time and by any means.
If interpreters may dismiss texts that conflict with their picture of Jesus, they lose any check on reshaping Jesus to fit their own preferences.
The early church rejected Marcion's separation of the Old Testament God from Christ, and Ancient Near Eastern conquest accounts show that totalizing war language was conventional hyperbole.

critiques.text: However it is qualified, a command to kill men, women, children and infants cannot be reconciled with the God who in Jesus loves enemies and dies for them; defending it as just risks justifying atrocity and fostering religious violence.
Treating every text as an equally clear window onto God ignores Hebrews' contrast between partial earlier revelation and the Son as the exact imprint of God's being.

A flat reading underplays the canon's movement and the newness of Christ: the Old Testament is true but incomplete, and the New Testament reinterprets holy war as spiritual struggle against powers, not flesh and blood.

responses.text: The commands were unique, tied to a specific moment of judgment and never a model for Christian conduct; and the hyperbolic reading shows they were less sweeping than they appear. The same Jesus who loves enemies will also judge the unrepentant, so love and judgment cannot be set against each other.
Hebrews contrasts the fullness of revelation, not its truthfulness: earlier revelation was partial, not false. 'Many portions and many ways' are still God speaking.
Whole-canon readers agree that the church does not wage holy war and that Christ redirects warfare to the spiritual realm; they deny only that this means the earlier wars misrepresented God.

strawMen.strawMan: This view endorses genocide and would justify it today.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders insist the conquest was a unique, divinely mandated judgment, not a precedent; most argue the commands were not genocide in the modern sense.

strawMen.strawMan: It ignores progressive revelation and reads Leviticus like the Gospels.
strawMen.correction: Most defenders affirm progressive revelation and the fulfillment of the law in Christ; they deny that later revelation shows earlier portraits of God to be wrong.

strawMen.strawMan: It holds that God is wrathful in the Old Testament and loving in the New.
strawMen.correction: It argues the opposite: God is both just and merciful in both Testaments (Exod 34:6-7; Rom 11:22).

positive: Preserves the unity and authority of the whole canon and a firm defense against Marcionism.
Takes divine holiness, justice and the seriousness of sin seriously.
Holds together the love and judgment of Jesus as presented in the New Testament.
negative: Can appear to defend the indefensible and alienate those troubled by violence.
Some historical forms were used to justify colonial and religious violence by analogy to the conquest.
Hyperbole arguments are disputed and may look like special pleading.

adherents: Most confessional Reformed and Presbyterian theologians
Many conservative evangelical and Baptist scholars
Classical Catholic and Lutheran theology (Augustine, Aquinas, Luther)
Evangelical apologists such as Paul Copan, William Lane Craig and Clay Jones

proponent.author: Tremper Longman III
proponent.title: "The Case for Spiritual Continuity" in Stanley N. Gundry, ed., Show Them No Mercy: Four Views on God and Canaanite Genocide

critic.author: Gregory A. Boyd
critic.title: The Crucifixion of the Warrior God

critic.author: C. S. Cowles
critic.title: "The Case for Radical Discontinuity" in Show Them No Mercy

sequence: Begin with the conviction that the text is God's word and reveals his character truly.
Read a judgment text (e.g. 1 Sam 15) in its historical setting: Ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric, the specific sin judged, and God's patience before acting.
Note its unique, unrepeatable role in Israel's history; it is not a model for Christian action.
Trace the theme forward: Israel's judgments foreshadow the final judgment and God's wrath against sin.
See the cross as the place where that wrath is borne for those who trust Christ, displaying God as just and justifier.
Apply it to final judgment: the returning Christ judges the unrepentant justly, and every judgment in Scripture anticipates that day.

positions.name: Christotelic progressive revelation
positions.summary: The canon is one story moving toward Christ as its goal (telos). The Old Testament must be reread in light of Christ, who fulfills and reconfigures it, but its texts are not overruled or written off as distortions. God's revelation is progressive: earlier portraits are true but partial, embedded in a particular moment of a long story, and they find their full meaning when read 'backwards' from the cross and resurrection.

figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
figures.profession: Bishop of Lyon; anti-Gnostic theologian
figures.bio: Against Marcion and the Gnostics, Irenaeus insisted that one God gave both covenants and that the Old Testament prepared humanity step by step for Christ, like a teacher educating a child. His picture of a progressive divine pedagogy summed up in Christ (recapitulation) underlies later christotelic reading.

figures.name: Brevard S. Childs
figures.profession: Old Testament scholar, Yale Divinity School
figures.bio: Childs's canonical approach insisted that the Old Testament be heard in its own voice as Christian Scripture and also read together with the New Testament in a two-Testament biblical theology, without collapsing either into the other.

works.author: Brevard S. Childs
works.title: Biblical Theology of the Old and New Testaments

figures.name: Richard B. Hays
figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Duke Divinity School
figures.bio: Hays argues that the Gospel writers teach readers to 'read backwards', discovering in Israel's Scriptures figures of Christ that could only be recognized after the resurrection, while also 'reading forwards' with the Old Testament's own integrity. He emphasizes figural reading in which both the Old Testament event and its fulfillment remain real.

works.author: Richard B. Hays
works.title: Reading Backwards: Figural Christology and the Fourfold Gospel Witness

works.author: Richard B. Hays
works.title: Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels

figures.name: Christopher J. H. Wright
figures.profession: Old Testament scholar; Global Ambassador of Langham Partnership
figures.bio: Wright confesses that the conquest remains deeply troubling and that he does not fully understand it, but argues it must be read as God's judgment within a larger story whose goal is blessing for all nations through Abraham's seed. He refuses both to justify the texts glibly and to set Christ against them.

works.author: Christopher J. H. Wright

positions.context:
This position draws on Irenaeus's divine pedagogy, Augustine's maxim that the New is concealed in the Old and the Old revealed in the New (*Questions on the Heptateuch* 2.73), and the Reformed tradition of redemptive-historical interpretation. In the twentieth century, biblical theology (Geerhardus Vos), the canonical approach (Brevard Childs) and studies of the New Testament's use of the Old (Richard Hays) gave it fresh form.

In the debate over Old Testament violence, it occupies the middle: with cruciform readers it insists that the meaning of Scripture is clarified in Christ and that the church does not wage holy war; with whole-canon readers it refuses to treat any Old Testament portrait of God as a distortion. Its defenders often leave room for lament and unresolved tension, as Christopher Wright does, rather than claiming a neat solution.
claims: The whole canon is a single story with Christ as its goal and climax.
Old Testament texts are true revelation, but partial and located in a particular stage of the story.
The New Testament rereads the Old figurally; meaning is clarified, not cancelled, by Christ.
Holy war in Israel was a unique stage of redemptive history, fulfilled in Christ's victory over evil powers.
Christ does not overrule Old Testament texts but shows their place and purpose.
Honest readers may lament what remains troubling without rejecting the text.

scriptures.reading: Jesus interprets 'all the Scriptures' concerning himself, showing that the Old Testament as a whole points to him.
Law, Prophets and Psalms are fulfilled in him; understanding requires that he open minds.
The Scriptures bear witness to Christ, and Moses wrote of him: witness, not error.
A veil remains over the reading of the old covenant until one turns to the Lord: Christ unveils the meaning that was there.
God really spoke through the prophets 'in many portions'; the Son completes rather than contradicts that speech.
Jesus came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them.
Israel's history was written down as types and warnings for those on whom the end of the ages has come.
From the start, the story aims at blessing all nations, the horizon in which even Israel's wars must be read.
Christ disarms the powers and triumphs over them by the cross: holy war is fulfilled in his victory.

arguments.text: Jesus and the apostles read the Old Testament as true witness to Christ, never as distortion; they also show that its meaning is fully grasped only after the resurrection.
The New Testament reconfigures Israel's warfare as the spiritual conflict of Christ and his people against evil powers, a fulfillment rather than a repeal.
The canon itself shows progressive revelation: concessions such as divorce and the stages of covenant law belong to particular moments that later revelation sets in context.
If Christ is the goal of the story, earlier chapters must be read in his light; but if earlier chapters could be false, the story would not truly lead to him.
Holding both the truth of the text and its incompleteness avoids two errors: letting modern intuitions overrule Scripture, and freezing earlier stages as timeless norms.
This was the church's answer to Marcion: one God, two Testaments, the Old read as Christian Scripture in light of Christ, as in Irenaeus and Augustine.

critiques.text: The middle view names the problem but leaves it unsolved: if the command to kill Amalekite infants is true revelation of God, then the God of Jesus did command it, and reading 'backwards' only relocates the difficulty.
Talk of 'partial' revelation and 'stages' can become a quiet way of relativizing texts; Scripture's portraits of God's judgment are not provisional but consistent from Genesis to Revelation.

Figural reading in the New Testament is selective; it does not establish that every violent portrait is a true picture of God, so the christotelic framework does not answer the moral question it raises.

responses.text: Christotelic readers accept that the tension is real and refuse to dissolve it either way; they argue the cross both affirms God's judgment on evil and reveals that he bears it himself, which is a deeper answer than denying the text.

'Partial' means incomplete, not untrue: the judgment theme is affirmed and fulfilled in Christ's victory and final judgment. The stages concern how God's purposes are carried out, not whether his character changes.

The aim is not to prove every text morally transparent to modern readers but to read each text faithfully within the whole story; some tension is the honest result, and lament is itself a biblical response.

strawMen.strawMan: This is just the flat view with nicer language.
strawMen.correction: It differs by treating Israel's holy war as a superseded stage fulfilled in spiritual warfare and by stressing figural rereading, not only historical defense.

strawMen.strawMan: It finds Jesus hidden in every verse by allegory.
strawMen.correction: Hays and Childs insist on the Old Testament's literal sense and its own voice; christological meaning comes through the story's direction and figural correspondence.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a cop-out that refuses to answer hard questions.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders give substantive answers about judgment and fulfillment, while admitting what remains mysterious.

sequence: Read the judgment text first in its own setting and literary context, hearing the Old Testament's own voice.
Locate it within the canon's story: promise to Abraham, Israel's calling, and God's purpose of blessing the nations.
Read 'backwards' from Christ: see how the New Testament takes up the theme (Israel's wars as figures of Christ's victory over evil powers).
Hold the text as true but partial, belonging to a stage of the story that Christ fulfills, so the church does not repeat it.
Apply it to final judgment: Christ, who bore judgment on the cross, will judge the world, and the Old Testament judgments foreshadow that day.
Where tension remains, respond with lament and trust rather than rejecting or flattening the text.

readings.reading: Earlier revelation was partial; the Son is the exact imprint of God, so the Son is the measure of every earlier portrait.
Both are God speaking; the contrast is between partial and full, not between false and true.
The verse describes a progressive story culminating in the Son, who completes what the prophets truly but partly said.
There is no God behind Jesus unlike Jesus; any portrait that conflicts with him must be reinterpreted.
Seeing Jesus is seeing the Father, including the Jesus who judges, rebukes and will return as judge.
Jesus reveals the Father fully, and that revelation illuminates the Old Testament rather than erasing it.
Jesus rejects Elijah's precedent of calling down fire: a model for correcting Old Testament portraits of God.
Jesus rebukes the disciples' vengeance against a village in a time of mercy, not Elijah's act; and the longer rebuke is textually uncertain.
The scene marks a new stage: in the time of the gospel's offer, judgment is deferred, not denied.
The command reflects Israel's culturally conditioned understanding of God, which he accommodated, not his true heart revealed in Christ.
A real command of God to judge entrenched idolatry, framed in hyperbolic war rhetoric and limited to that moment.
A true but partial stage in God's war against evil, fulfilled in Christ's victory over the powers and not repeated by the church.
The command to kill infants is incompatible with the God revealed on the cross and must be read as a human-shaped portrait God allowed.
Judgment on Amalek's long history of attacking the weak; God as Judge may take life, and the language may be stylized.
A deeply troubling text that belongs to Israel's unique theocratic history; it is held in tension, awaiting Christ who bears judgment himself.
God's righteousness is shown in self-giving love that overcomes sin rather than in retributive violence.
The cross shows God both just and justifier, upholding wrath against sin rather than abolishing it.
God's earlier 'passing over' of sins finds its meaning in the cross, which interprets the whole history of judgment and mercy.
The rider's robe is dipped in his own blood before the battle, and his sword comes from his mouth: he conquers by the word and the cross.
The returning Christ is the warrior-judge who treads the winepress of God's wrath; judgment is not foreign to Jesus.
Israel's holy war reaches its final fulfillment in Christ's eschatological victory, carried out by him alone.
Jesus overrides 'eye for eye' and grounds enemy love in the Father's character: God is like this.
Jesus corrects personal vengeance, not God's judicial authority; the same Sermon warns of judgment.
Jesus fulfills the law by revealing its deepest intent for his community, a new stage rather than a repudiation.

timeline.title: Marcion separated from the Roman church
timeline.note: Marcion rejects the Old Testament and its God as distinct from the Father of Jesus; the church's rejection of him shapes all later debate.

timeline.title: Irenaeus's Against Heresies
timeline.note: One God of both covenants, revealed progressively and summed up in Christ.

timeline.title: Origen's Homilies on Joshua
timeline.note: The conquest read spiritually as the Christian's warfare against sin (date approximate).

timeline.title: Augustine's Against Faustus
timeline.note: Augustine defends Israel's wars and the unity of the Testaments against Manichean critique (date approximate).

timeline.title: Luther's preface to James and Jude
timeline.note: Luther makes 'what promotes Christ' a test of apostolic writing, an early Protestant christocentric criterion.

timeline.title: Calvin's Commentary on Joshua
timeline.note: Calvin defends the conquest as just judgment while acknowledging its apparent cruelty.

timeline.title: Barth's Church Dogmatics begins
timeline.note: Barth makes Christ the center and criterion of all theology, influencing later christocentric hermeneutics.

timeline.title: Childs's Biblical Theology of the Old and New Testaments
timeline.note: A canonical, two-Testament approach to reading Christian Scripture.

timeline.title: Show Them No Mercy: Four Views
timeline.note: C. S. Cowles (radical discontinuity), Eugene Merrill, Daniel Gard and Tremper Longman debate the conquest.

timeline.title: Enns's Inspiration and Incarnation
timeline.note: Popularizes 'christotelic' reading of apostolic hermeneutics.

timeline.title: Christopher Wright's The God I Don't Understand
timeline.note: A middle path that admits unresolved difficulty while rejecting both glib defense and christological rejection.

timeline.title: Seibert and Jones sharpen the debate
timeline.note: Seibert's *Disturbing Divine Behavior* and Clay Jones's Philosophia Christi article stake out opposite poles.

timeline.title: Copan's Is God a Moral Monster?
timeline.note: A popular defense of Old Testament ethics, including the hyperbole reading of conquest texts.

timeline.title: Hays's Reading Backwards; Copan and Flannagan
timeline.note: Figural christology and a detailed defense of the conquest commands appear the same year.

timeline.title: Boyd's Crucifixion of the Warrior God
timeline.note: The most extensive statement of the cruciform hermeneutic.

argumentMap.text: Jesus crucified is the lens for every portrait of God in Scripture.
The Son is the exact imprint of God's nature; earlier revelation was partial.
Jesus himself corrected Old Testament precedents.
Setting Christ against Old Testament portraits of God drifts toward Marcionism.
Cruciform readers keep the whole Old Testament as inspired and affirm one God; Marcion rejected both.
Jesus and the apostles read Old Testament portraits as true witness, not distortion.
Jesus did call some provisions concessions to hard hearts.
Every text reveals God truly; the conquest was a just judgment.
God waited for the Amorites' iniquity to be complete.
The New Testament Jesus is also judge and warrior.
Commanding the death of infants cannot be reconciled with the God who loves enemies.
The language is stylized war rhetoric and the command unique; God as Judge may take life.
The rider's robe is dipped in his own blood; he conquers by the word.
Read the canon toward Christ without overruling Old Testament texts.
Jesus interprets all the Scriptures concerning himself.
Holy war is fulfilled in Christ's victory over the powers.
Reading backwards relocates the moral problem without solving it.
The cross both affirms judgment on evil and shows God bearing it himself.
Talk of 'partial' stages can relativize Scripture's consistent portrait of judgment.
Partial means incomplete, not untrue; God's character does not change, his methods do.
